claim: In 2018, an estimated 228 million malaria cases occurred worldwide.
source: In 2018, according to the WHO, 2019 published by the WHO, an estimated 228 million malaria cases occurred worldwide, with an estimated 405,000 deaths from malaria globally (WHO, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to WHO, 2019.

claim: In 2018, an estimated 405,000 deaths from malaria occurred globally.
source: In 2018, according to the WHO, 2019 published by the WHO, an estimated 228 million malaria cases occurred worldwide, with an estimated 405,000 deaths from malaria globally (WHO, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to WHO, 2019.

claim: Most malaria cases in 2018 occurred in sub-Saharan Africa.
source: In 2018, according to the WHO, 2019 published by the WHO, an estimated 228 million malaria cases occurred worldwide, with an estimated 405,000 deaths from malaria globally (WHO, 2019).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to WHO, 2019 and is stated in the abstract.

claim: Around 85 million pregnancies occurred in 2007 in areas with stable Plasmodium falciparum transmission.
source: Dellicour et al., 2010 estimated that around 85 million pregnancies occurred in 2007 in areas with stable Plasmodium falciparum (one of the most prevalent malaria parasites) transmission and therefore were at risk of malaria.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Dellicour et al., 2010.

claim: Pregnant women are particularly susceptible to malaria even if they have developed immunity from childhood infections.
source: Pregnant women are particularly susceptible to malaria, even if they have developed immunity from childhood infections, in part because parasitized cells in the placenta express unique variant surface antigens (Rogerson et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Rogerson et al., 2007.

claim: Parasitized cells in the placenta express unique variant surface antigens.
source: Pregnant women are particularly susceptible to malaria, even if they have developed immunity from childhood infections, in part because parasitized cells in the placenta express unique variant surface antigens (Rogerson et al., 2007).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Rogerson et al., 2007.

claim: Malaria parasites exacerbate maternal anemia.
source: Parasites exacerbate maternal anemia and they also sequester in the placenta, leading to intrauterine growth restriction, low birth weight (i.e. birth weight <2500 g), preterm delivery and even stillbirth and neonatal death.
evidence: The claim is stated as an established fact in the introduction.

claim: Malaria parasites sequester in the placenta, leading to intrauterine growth restriction, low birth weight, preterm delivery, stillbirth and neonatal death.
source: Parasites exacerbate maternal anemia and they also sequester in the placenta, leading to intrauterine growth restriction, low birth weight (i.e. birth weight <2500 g), preterm delivery and even stillbirth and neonatal death.
evidence: The claim is stated as an established fact in the introduction.

claim: Preventing malaria during pregnancy with drugs or insecticide treated nets has a significant impact on pregnancy outcomes.
source: Preventing malaria during pregnancy with drugs or insecticide treated nets has a significant impact on pregnancy outcomes (Eisele et al., 2012; Kayentao et al., 2013; Radeva-Petrova et al., 2014).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Eisele et al., 2012; Kayentao et al., 2013; Radeva-Petrova et al., 2014.

claim: Early exposure to Plasmodium falciparum (before 120 days gestation) was associated with a reduction in birth weight of more than 200 g.
source: However, in one study, early exposure to Plasmodium falciparum (before 120 days gestation), prior to initiating malaria prevention measures, was associated with a reduction in birth weight of more than 200 g and reduced average gestational age of nearly 1 week (Schmiegelow et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Schmiegelow et al., 2017.

claim: Early exposure to Plasmodium falciparum (before 120 days gestation) reduced average gestational age of nearly 1 week.
source: However, in one study, early exposure to Plasmodium falciparum (before 120 days gestation), prior to initiating malaria prevention measures, was associated with a reduction in birth weight of more than 200 g and reduced average gestational age of nearly 1 week (Schmiegelow et al., 2017).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Schmiegelow et al., 2017.

claim: Global cases of malaria declined by an estimated 41% between 2000 and 2015.
source: Although the magnitude of the decline is difficult to estimate precisely, some reports suggest that the global cases of malaria declined by an estimated 41% between 2000 and 2015 (WHO, 2016) and the clinical cases of Plasmodium falciparum malaria declined by 40% in Africa between 2000 and 2015 (Bhatt et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to WHO, 2016.

claim: Clinical cases of Plasmodium falciparum malaria declined by 40% in Africa between 2000 and 2015.
source: Although the magnitude of the decline is difficult to estimate precisely, some reports suggest that the global cases of malaria declined by an estimated 41% between 2000 and 2015 (WHO, 2016) and the clinical cases of Plasmodium falciparum malaria declined by 40% in Africa between 2000 and 2015 (Bhatt et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bhatt et al., 2015.

claim: Low birth weight is strongly associated with poor cognitive and physical development of children.
source: Understanding the potential causal effect of a reduction in malaria burden on the low birth weight rate is crucial as low birth weight is strongly associated with poor cognitive and physical development of children (McCormick et al., 1992; Avchen et al., 2001; Guyatt and Snow, 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to McCormick et al., 1992; Avchen et al., 2001; Guyatt and Snow, 2004.

claim: The study analyzed data from 18,112 births in 19 countries in sub-Saharan African countries during the years 2000–2015.
source: We conducted an observational study of the effect of changing malaria burden on low birth weight using data from 18,112 births in 19 countries in sub-Saharan African countries during the years 2000–2015.
evidence: The claim is stated in the abstract and methods section.

claim: A malaria prevalence decline from a high rate (PfPR2-10 > 0.4) to a low rate (PfPR2-10 < 0.2) is estimated to reduce the rate of low birth weight by 1.48 percentage points (95% confidence interval: 3.70 percentage points reduction, 0.74 percentage points increase).
source: A malaria prevalence decline from a high rate (Plasmodium falciparum parasite rate in children aged 2-up-to-10 (i.e. PfPR2-10) > 0.4) to a low rate (PfPR2-10 < 0.2) is estimated to reduce the rate of low birth weight by 1.48 percentage points (95% confidence interval: 3.70 percentage points reduction, 0.74 percentage points increase), which is a 17% reduction in the low birth weight rate compared to the average (8.6%) in our study population with observed birth weight records (1.48/8.6 ≈ 17%).
evidence: The claim is supported by the study's primary analysis results.

claim: The estimated 1.48 percentage point reduction in low birth weight rate represents a 17% reduction compared to the average (8.6%) in the study population with observed birth weight records.
source: A malaria prevalence decline from a high rate (Plasmodium falciparum parasite rate in children aged 2-up-to-10 (i.e. PfPR2-10) > 0.4) to a low rate (PfPR2-10 < 0.2) is estimated to reduce the rate of low birth weight by 1.48 percentage points (95% confidence interval: 3.70 percentage points reduction, 0.74 percentage points increase), which is a 17% reduction in the low birth weight rate compared to the average (8.6%) in our study population with observed birth weight records (1.48/8.6 ≈ 17%).
evidence: The claim is supported by the study's primary analysis results and calculation.

claim: For first pregnancies, a decline in malaria prevalence from high to low is estimated to reduce the low birth weight rate by 3.73 percentage points (95% confidence interval: 9.11 percentage points reduction, 1.64 percentage points increase).
source: When focusing on first pregnancies, a decline in malaria prevalence from high to low is estimated to have a greater impact on the low birth weight rate than for all births: 3.73 percentage points (95% confidence interval: 9.11 percentage points reduction, 1.64 percentage points increase).
evidence: The claim is supported by the study's secondary analysis results.

claim: The year 2000 marked a turning point in multilateral commitment to malaria control in sub-Saharan Africa.
source: Second, according to Bhatt et al., 2015, 'the year 2000 marked a turning point in multilateral commitment to malaria control in sub-Saharan Africa, catalysed by the Roll Back Malaria initiative and the wider development agenda around the United Nations Millennium Development Goals'.
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Bhatt et al., 2015.

claim: The mean Haversine distance of the early year clusters and late year clusters is 24.1 km among the 219 high-low pairs of clusters.
source: Of note, the mean Haversine distance of the early year clusters and late year clusters is 24.1 km among the 219 high-low pairs of clusters, and 28.7 km among the 219 high-high pairs of clusters.
evidence: The claim is supported by the study's matching results reported in Table 4.

claim: The mean Haversine distance of the early year clusters and late year clusters is 28.7 km among the 219 high-high pairs of clusters.
source: Of note, the mean Haversine distance of the early year clusters and late year clusters is 24.1 km among the 219 high-low pairs of clusters, and 28.7 km among the 219 high-high pairs of clusters.
evidence: The claim is supported by the study's matching results reported in Table 4.

claim: Among the study individuals with nonmissing birth weight, the low birth weight rate was 8.6%.
source: Among the 9603 records with observed birth weight, 825 (8.6%) had low birth weight.
evidence: The claim is supported by the study's data analysis.

claim: 48% of the birth weight records of children among the 18,499 records are missing.
source: However, 48% of the birth weight records of children among these 18,499 records are missing.
evidence: The claim is supported by the study's data description.

claim: Mother's reported size of the child is a powerful tool to handle the missing data problem with birth weight.
source: The mother's reported size of the child is relatively complete in the IPUMS-DHS data set and has been shown to be a powerful tool to handle the missing data problem with birth weight (Blanc and Wardlaw, 2005).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Blanc and Wardlaw, 2005.

claim: Mother's age, child's birth order, mother's education level, and the mother's reported birth size are significant predictors of low birth weight in the imputation model.
source: From Table 2, we can see that in the imputation model, mother's age, child's birth order, mother's education level, and the mother's reported birth size are significant predictors, which agrees with the previous literature (e.g. Fraser et al., 1995; Strobino et al., 1995; Richards et al., 2001; Valero De Bernabé et al., 2004).
evidence: The claim is supported by the study's imputation model results in Table 2 and citations to previous literature.

claim: Mothers with higher education level are less likely to deliver a child with low birth weight.
source: For example, mothers with higher education level are less likely to deliver a child with low birth weight, and boys are less likely to have low birth weight than girls, which agrees with the previous literature (e.g. Brooke et al., 1989; Valero De Bernabé et al., 2004; Zeka et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by the study's results and citations to previous literature.

claim: Boys are less likely to have low birth weight than girls.
source: For example, mothers with higher education level are less likely to deliver a child with low birth weight, and boys are less likely to have low birth weight than girls, which agrees with the previous literature (e.g. Brooke et al., 1989; Valero De Bernabé et al., 2004; Zeka et al., 2008).
evidence: The claim is supported by the study's results and citations to previous literature.

claim: The effects of malaria on birth outcomes are most pronounced in the first pregnancy.
source: This agrees with previous studies which demonstrate that the effects of malaria on birth outcomes are most pronounced in the first pregnancy (e.g. McGregor et al., 1983).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to McGregor et al., 1983.

claim: The observed low birth weight rate among records with observed birth weight within the early year clusters in high-low pairs is 9.33%.
source: The observed low birth weight rates among the records with observed birth weight within the early year clusters in high-low pairs is 9.33%, in the late year clusters in high-low pairs is 7.52%, in the early year clusters in high-high pairs is 9.18%, and in the late year clusters in high-high pairs is 9.06%.
evidence: The claim is supported by the study's data analysis.

claim: The observed low birth weight rate among records with observed birth weight within the late year clusters in high-low pairs is 7.52%.
source: The observed low birth weight rates among the records with observed birth weight within the early year clusters in high-low pairs is 9.33%, in the late year clusters in high-low pairs is 7.52%, in the early year clusters in high-high pairs is 9.18%, and in the late year clusters in high-high pairs is 9.06%.
evidence: The claim is supported by the study's data analysis.

claim: The observed low birth weight rate among records with observed birth weight within the early year clusters in high-high pairs is 9.18%.
source: The observed low birth weight rates among the records with observed birth weight within the early year clusters in high-low pairs is 9.33%, in the late year clusters in high-low pairs is 7.52%, in the early year clusters in high-high pairs is 9.18%, and in the late year clusters in high-high pairs is 9.06%.
evidence: The claim is supported by the study's data analysis.

claim: The observed low birth weight rate among records with observed birth weight within the late year clusters in high-high pairs is 9.06%.
source: The observed low birth weight rates among the records with observed birth weight within the early year clusters in high-low pairs is 9.33%, in the late year clusters in high-low pairs is 7.52%, in the early year clusters in high-high pairs is 9.18%, and in the late year clusters in high-high pairs is 9.06%.
evidence: The claim is supported by the study's data analysis.

claim: The naive difference-in-differences estimator for the effect of reduced malaria burden without adjusting for covariates and missingness of birth weight records is 1.69 percentage points reduction on the low birth weight rate.
source: Therefore, the naive difference-in-differences estimator for the effect of reduced malaria burden without adjusting for covariates and missingness of birth weight records is (7.52% − 9.33%) − (9.06% − 9.18%) = − 1.69% (i.e. 1.69 percentage points reduction on the low birth weight rate).
evidence: The claim is supported by the study's calculation based on observed data.

claim: Among all the high-low pairs of clusters in the sample, there has been a decrease in the low birth weight rate from the early years to the late years of 1.81 percentage points for records with observed birth weight.
source: Among all the high-low pairs of clusters in our sample, there has been a decrease in the low birth weight rate from the early years to the late years of 1.81 percentage points (from 9.33% to 7.52%) for records with observed birth weight and an estimated decrease of 2.04 percentage points (from 10.48% to 8.44%) when multiple imputation is used to impute missing birth weight records.
evidence: The claim is supported by the study's data analysis.

claim: Among all the high-low pairs of clusters in the sample, there has been an estimated decrease in the low birth weight rate from the early years to the late years of 2.04 percentage points when multiple imputation is used to impute missing birth weight records.
source: Among all the high-low pairs of clusters in our sample, there has been a decrease in the low birth weight rate from the early years to the late years of 1.81 percentage points (from 9.33% to 7.52%) for records with observed birth weight and an estimated decrease of 2.04 percentage points (from 10.48% to 8.44%) when multiple imputation is used to impute missing birth weight records.
evidence: The claim is supported by the study's data analysis with multiple imputation.

claim: The estimated effect of the time indicator (late year vs. early year) is a 0.06 percentage points reduction in low birth weight rate.
source: The estimated effect in Table 6 of the time indicator (late year vs. early year) is a 0.06 percentage points reduction, which is much less than that of the low malaria prevalence indicator.
evidence: The claim is supported by the study's regression results in Table 6.

claim: The estimated change in the low birth weight rate over time among high-low pairs that comes from changes in the covariates over time is a 0.52 percentage points reduction.
source: Moreover, the estimated change in the low birth weight rate over time among high-low pairs that comes from changes in the covariates over time is a 0.52 percentage points reduction.
evidence: The claim is supported by the study's calculation based on regression coefficients.

claim: The reductions in low birth weight rate from early year to late year among the high-low pairs are considerably greater than those among high-high pairs.
source: From Figure 3, we can see that although in general, for both high-high pairs and high-low pairs, the birth weight rates of the late year clusters are lower than those of the early year clusters, it is clear that the reductions in low birth weight rate from early year to late year among the high-low pairs are considerably greater than those among high-high pairs, suggesting that reducing community-level malaria burden can potentially substantially reduce the low birth weight rate.
evidence: The claim is supported by visual evidence in Figure 3 and the study's interpretation.

claim: Reducing community-level malaria burden can potentially substantially reduce the low birth weight rate.
source: From Figure 3, we can see that although in general, for both high-high pairs and high-low pairs, the birth weight rates of the late year clusters are lower than those of the early year clusters, it is clear that the reductions in low birth weight rate from early year to late year among the high-low pairs are considerably greater than those among high-high pairs, suggesting that reducing community-level malaria burden can potentially substantially reduce the low birth weight rate.
evidence: The claim is inferred from the study's data analysis and visual evidence in Figure 3.

claim: The magnitude of the estimated effect of a reduction from high malaria prevalence to low malaria prevalence on the low birth weight rate (1.48 percentage points) is greater than the estimated effect of antenatal care during pregnancy (0.96 percentage points).
source: Although we cannot rule out no effect at a 95% confidence level, the magnitude of the estimated effect of a reduction from high malaria prevalence to low malaria prevalence on the low birth weight rate (1.48 percentage points) is even greater than the estimated effect of a factor thought to be important, antenatal care during pregnancy (0.96 percentage points).
evidence: The claim is supported by comparing the study's regression results.

claim: Previous studies have shown that individual malaria prevention during pregnancy reduces the chances of the woman's baby having low birth weight.
source: Previous studies have shown that individual malaria prevention during pregnancy reduces the chances of the woman's baby having low birth weight (Kayentao et al., 2013).
evidence: The claim is supported by a citation to Kayentao et al., 2013.

claim: Reports of declining malaria mortality underestimate the contribution of reduced malaria exposure during pregnancy on pregnancy outcomes and neonatal survival.
source: Furthermore, we conclude that reports of declining malaria mortality underestimate the contribution of reduced malaria exposure during pregnancy on pregnancy outcomes and neonatal survival.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings.

claim: Overall reduction in exposure to malaria infection, including during pregnancy, outweighs individual changes in risk once infected.
source: Although some studies have documented higher rates of adverse pregnancy outcomes in malaria-infected women with declining antimalarial immunity, such as may be seen in communities with declining malaria exposure (Mayor et al., 2015), our study demonstrates that overall reduction in exposure to infection, including during pregnancy, outweighs these individual changes in risk once infected.
evidence: The claim is a conclusion drawn from the study's findings, with reference to Mayor et al., 2015.

claim: Within each country the DHS samples different locations (clusters) over different survey years.
source: The DHS collects data from different clusters within the same country in different survey years.
evidence: The claim is stated as a characteristic of the DHS data.

claim: A total of 950 out of 6812 pairs of clusters met the criteria for being high-high or high-low pairs, with 540 being high-high pairs and 410 high-low pairs.
source: A total of 950 out of 6812 pairs of clusters met one of these two criteria with 540 being high-high pairs and 410 high-low pairs.
evidence: The claim is supported by the study's data selection process.

claim: After implementing the optimal cardinality matching, 219 matched quadruples (pairs of high-low and high-high pairs of clusters) remain.
source: After implementing the optimal cardinality matching, 219 matched quadruples (pairs of high-low and high-high pairs of clusters) remain.
evidence: The claim is supported by the study's matching procedure.

claim: Among the 19,310 children's records from the quadruples formed, multiple births (i.e. twins, triplets etc) were excluded, leaving 18,499 records.
source: Among all the 19,310 children's records from the quadruples formed above, we exclude multiple births (i.e. twins, triplets etc), leaving 18,499 records.
evidence: The claim is supported by the study's data processing steps.

claim: After excluding records with missing mother's subjective reported size of the child, 18,112 records remain, 47% of which (8509 records) have missing low birth weight indicator.
source: We exclude the small number of records with missing mother's subjective reported size of the child, leaving 18,112 records, 47% of which (8509 records) have missing low birth weight indicator.
evidence: The claim is supported by the study's data processing steps.

claim: The study used 500 replications for multiple imputation.
source: To handle this, we perform multiple imputation, under the assumption of missing at random (Heitjan and Basu, 1996), with 500 replications.
evidence: The claim is stated in the methods section.

claim: The study period was set to be the years 2000–2015.
source: In this article, we set the study period to be the years 2000–2015, and correspondingly, all the results and conclusions obtained in this article are limited to the years 2000–2015.
evidence: The claim is stated in the methods section.

claim: The years 2000–2007 were defined as the 'early years' and the years 2008–2015 as the 'late years'.
source: After selecting 2000–2015 as our study period, we take the middle point years 2007 and 2008 as the cut-off and define the years 2000–2007 as the 'early years' and the years 2008–2015 as the 'late years.'
evidence: The claim is stated in the methods section.

claim: 19 sub-Saharan African countries met the eligibility criteria for the study.
source: The 19 sub-Saharan African countries that meet the above eligibility criteria are listed in Table 1.
evidence: The claim is supported by the study's data selection procedure and Table 1.

claim: Before matching, the high-low pairs tend to be sociodemographically better off than the high-high pairs.
source: From Table 5, we can see that before matching, the high-high pairs are quite different from the high-low pairs, all absolute standardized differences are greater than 0.2. The high-low pairs tend to be sociodemographically better off than the high-high pairs (higher prevalence of improved toilet facilities and floor material facilities, higher prevalence of domestic electricity, higher levels of mother's education, higher rate of contraceptive use, and more urban households).
evidence: The claim is supported by the study's matching results in Table 5.

claim: After matching, all 12 covariates are balanced well with all absolute standardized differences less than 0.1.
source: After matching, we can see that all 12 covariates are balanced well – all absolute standardized differences after matching are less than 0.1.
evidence: The claim is supported by the study's matching results in Table 5.

claim: The within-pair longitudes' and latitudes' correlations between the paired early year and late year clusters among the high-low and high-high pairs are all nearly one.
source: The within-pair longitudes' and latitudes' correlations between the paired early year and late year clusters among the high-low and high-high pairs are all nearly one.
evidence: The claim is supported by the study's matching results in Table 4.

claim: Declining transmission of malaria will lead to reductions in maternal immunity to malaria.
source: However, declining transmission will also lead to reductions in maternal immunity to malaria.
evidence: The claim is stated as an expected consequence in the introduction.

claim: Maternal immunity is important in mitigating the effects of malaria infection during pregnancy.
source: Maternal immunity is important in mitigating the effects of malaria infection during pregnancy as is evidenced by the reduced impact of malaria exposure on the second, third and subsequent pregnancies.
evidence: The claim is stated as established knowledge in the introduction.

claim: The impact of malaria exposure is reduced on the second, third and subsequent pregnancies compared to the first pregnancy.
source: Maternal immunity is important in mitigating the effects of malaria infection during pregnancy as is evidenced by the reduced impact of malaria exposure on the second, third and subsequent pregnancies.
evidence: The claim is stated as evidence for the importance of maternal immunity.

claim: There is a complex relationship between declining malaria exposure and pregnancy outcomes that depends on both current transmission and historical transmission and community-level immunity.
source: Thus, we anticipate a complex relationship between declining exposure and pregnancy outcomes that depends on both current transmission and historical transmission and community-level immunity (Mayor et al., 2015).
evidence: The claim is stated as an expectation with reference to Mayor et al., 2015.

claim: The study used optimal matching to pair two DHS clusters, one in the early year and one in the late year as closely as possible.
source: We use optimal matching (Rosenbaum, 1989; Hansen and Klopfer, 2006) to pair two DHS clusters, one in the early year and one in the late year as closely as possible, mimicking a single DHS cluster measured twice in two different time periods.
evidence: The claim is stated in the methods section with citations to Rosenbaum, 1989; Hansen and Klopfer, 2006.

claim: The difference-in-differences approach removes bias from three potential sources: (1) time-invariant differences between treated and control units, (2) trends over time that affect both treated and control units equally, and (3) regression to the mean.
source: The difference-in-differences approach (Card and Krueger, 2000; Angrist and Pischke, 2008; Dimick and Ryan, 2014; St. Clair and Cook, 2015) compares the changes in the low birth weight rate over time for treated units (i.e. high-low pairs of clusters) compared to control units (i.e. high-high pairs of clusters) adjusted for observed covariates. The difference-in-differences approach removes bias from three potential sources (Volpp et al., 2007):
evidence: The claim is stated in the methods section with citations to Card and Krueger, 2000; Angrist and Pischke, 2008; Dimick and Ryan, 2014; St. Clair and Cook, 2015; Volpp et al., 2007.

claim: The traditional difference-in-differences approach requires a parallel trend assumption.
source: The traditional difference-in-differences approach requires a parallel trend assumption, which states that the path of the outcome (e.g. the low birth weight rate) for the treated unit is parallel to that for the control unit (Card and Krueger, 2000; Angrist and Pischke, 2008; Dimick and Ryan, 2014; St. Clair and Cook, 2015).
evidence: The claim is stated in the methods section with citations to Card and Krueger, 2000; Angrist and Pischke, 2008; Dimick and Ryan, 2014; St. Clair and Cook, 2015.

claim: Using matching as a nonparametric data preprocessing step in a difference-in-differences study can remove bias caused by survey location sampling variability.
source: Using matching as a nonparametric data preprocessing step in a difference-in-differences study can remove this type of bias because the observed covariates trajectories are forced to be common among the matched treated and control groups (St. Clair and Cook, 2015; Basu and Small, 2020).
evidence: The claim is stated in the methods section with citations to St. Clair and Cook, 2015; Basu and Small, 2020.

claim: Multiple imputation constructs several plausible imputed data sets and appropriately combines results obtained from each of them to obtain valid inferences under an assumption that the data is missing at random conditional on measured covariates.
source: Multiple imputation constructs several plausible imputed data sets and appropriately combines results obtained from each of them to obtain valid inferences under an assumption that the data is missing at random conditional on measured covariates (Rubin, 1987).
evidence: The claim is stated in the methods section with a citation to Rubin, 1987.

claim: Failing to carefully and appropriately address the missing data issue with the birth weight records can significantly bias the estimates of the low birth weight rate derived from surveys in developing countries.
source: The fraction of missingness in birth weight in the IPUMS-DHS data set is non-negligible and previous studies have noted that failing to carefully and appropriately address the missing data issue with the birth weight records can significantly bias the estimates of the low birth weight rate derived from surveys in developing countries (Boerma et al., 1996; Robles and Goldman, 1999).
evidence: The claim is supported by citations to Boerma et al., 1996; Robles and Goldman, 1999.
